chapters.title: Epstein speaks on dog run composting pilot program

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: As Councilmember Hank said, I have a shitty bill going on here.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So I want to thank the speaker for advancing this package, this group act package, my bill 864.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We talk about the issue of dog waste.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: People may not know about New York City dogs produce about 500,000 pounds of dog waste a day.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: 500,000 pounds of dog waste a day.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So, you know, we've seen, as Council Member Hanif talked about during the storm this year, a surge in dog waste complaints, 300 from 301 complaints.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You know, that's why this good gap came together.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: For us, this opportunity to divert dog waste from landfills is a really important opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If we get every dog run to have their own diversion program, not only do we divert a lot of this dog waste because a lot of people use these dog runs, but we reduce methane gas, greenhouse gases in our environment.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So it's a lot of wins of making sure we reduce our landfill.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We empower people in dog runs to effectuate a plan, and we provide...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: provide better soil for New York.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's a win-win all around.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I really would applaud the speaker, the advocates, and my colleagues to make this happen.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Menin introduces Intro 880 by Council Member Narcisse, requiring signage at park entrances and facilities stating the prohibition on leaving dog waste and associated penalties.
chapters.title: Menin introduces Narcisse's dog waste signage bill

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And the next package, next bill in the package is Introduction 880, sponsored by Councilmember Mercedes Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And this bill would require signage at the entrances and exits of parks and at certain park facilities, stating the rule prohibiting a person from leaving dog waste on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And also there will be penalties for doing so.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I invite Councilmember Narcisse to talk about her bill.

chapters.summary: Narcisse thanks Menin for supporting Haitian New Yorkers amid TPS termination, then presents her bill requiring clear signage at parks telling dog owners to pick up waste, noting the unfair burden on parks staff who clean up before visitors arrive.
chapters.title: Narcisse speaks on park signage bill and addresses Haitian community crisis

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And before I get to the scoop, I want to say thank you for acknowledging what Haitians are going through in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And if you have questions how government works, if you have doubts or believe how government can help you out, if you're out there, this is how it is.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Not only that you took the fight on, you stood up with us and saying that those folks that here need fairness.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We cannot change the federal because we're not federal, but standing together and the mayors as well stood up and see what the Haitian going through.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Those are the folks that came here legally that was asked to come here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And unfortunately, they get cut between what's going on, the politics, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Am I in support of making sure we have immigration reform?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And that's where you meet, like when you're Haitian and then you're American and you're in government.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Now I have to represent the community where I was elected to do my job.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But at the same time, I have to have sympathy and empathy for what's going on with my native land.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Having said all that, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Adam Speaker for helping me out, for seeing what's the Haitian going through.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And what can I say?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm sad, but I have to keep on doing my work here, what I was elected to do.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Walk through even my parks, Marine Park, Canarsie Park, and my district, and everywhere in town.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You have, in the parks, you have seen it, you have smelled it, and you've been upset about it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What's going on in our parks?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We need to do better, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If you in my parks, Canarsie Park, my district, or nearly any other parks in our city, and you will see kids on the grass, families with strollers and dog waste that somebody decided was not their problem,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: parks staff are out there cleaning it up before the rest of us get up.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's unfair to them.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: My bill, Intro 880, puts signs at park entrances and playgrounds and other facilities inside the park.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In plain language, plain, simple language, pick up after your dog or pick up your SHIT.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Here is the fine if you don't.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The rest of the package comes at the same...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Problem from other angles.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Most dogs owners already do the right thing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I have to say, I love dogs.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: My kids had so many that I had to take care of.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And yeah, I love dogs.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: These bills are for the ones, you know, counting on nobody seeing them.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You know, you have seen them at your windows where they see the poops and they try to run and separate themselves from it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So now we have a way to say, no, this is yours.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Pick it up.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Most dog owners doing it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So we want everyone to do it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So Madam Speaker, thank you again.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I know while I'm in the crisis for the Haitian, and I still have to talk about what's going on in our city.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: God bless.

chapters.summary: Menin introduces Intro 857A requiring Sanitation to install and fill dog waste bag dispensers on at least 1,200 public litter baskets, and notes the Office of Insurance Affordability bill (Intro 685B) will also be voted on.
chapters.title: Menin introduces her own dog waste bag dispenser bill and insurance office bill

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then the last bill in the package, Introduction 857A, sponsored by myself, would require the Department of Sanitation to install and regularly fill dog waste bag dispensers on at least 1,200

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: public litter baskets on city streets.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And now I'm going to move on to the other bills that we are voting on today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 685B, which I talked about earlier, would establish an Office of Insurance Affordability to support consumers navigating the insurance market and address the rising cost of insurance.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And now we will move on to the hot topic of outdoor dining.

chapters.summary: Menin introduces Intro 655A by Council Member Restler, expanding the outdoor dining program by removing seasonal restrictions on roadway cafe operations.
chapters.title: Menin introduces Restler's year-round outdoor dining bill

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 655-A, sponsored by Councilmember Lincoln Ressler, would expand the city's outdoor dining program by removing seasonal restrictions on roadway cafe operation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I invite Councilmember Ressler to come up.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Restler details how the seasonal program caused a 90% decline in outdoor dining participation due to prohibitive construction and storage costs. His bill restores year-round dining with design flexibility, an 11 p.m. closing time, accountability for repeat violators, and maintained cleanliness standards.
chapters.title: Restler speaks on restoring year-round outdoor dining

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's great to join.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Should I?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: No, we don't have anything for me to roll out today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay, too bad for the vertically challenged among us.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's great to join such a robust class of council interns and all of you today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just firstly want to thank Speaker Menin.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Long before she was speaker, she has been eagerly conspiring with me to fix the outdoor dining program and I think has been the single most enthusiastic supporter at my side to restore year-round outdoor dining in the city council.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I really just want to thank her for her leadership.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: At every step of the way, she has said, I have your back.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're going to get this done.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is important, and I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It was about three years ago that the city council, that the Adams era program for seasonal outdoor dining was approved.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it nearly broke outdoor dining in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We saw a 90% decline in the number of restaurants that used to offer outdoor dining and that no longer did.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And the explanation for why restaurants no longer offer outdoor dining is simple.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It became stupidly expensive.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Stupidly expensive to have to build, deconstruct, and store these outdoor dining structures every year.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For small neighborhood restaurants, it was just infeasible.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Today, we are fixing that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We are going to restore outdoor dining to its previous glory with thousands of additional

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: outdoor dining establishments, we anticipate opening up across the five boroughs, which is great for our local economy, great for our neighborhood businesses, great for our workforce, great for all of us to enjoy a meal outdoors.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Controller Lander did a study a couple years ago that found for every restaurant that adds outdoor dining, we create a job.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And at a time when the New York City private sector workforce is

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: shrinking, with the exception of home health aides, we really need good jobs across our communities.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There are some additional changes that I think are really positive in our legislation that will help more businesses participate in the program.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We are making some modifications to the design to allow for some vertical elements to exist around outdoor dining structures and overhead structures as well.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: While we're not returning to the era of sheds, we are making it more comfortable for people to enjoy outdoor dining during winter months or during inclement weather year-round.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're also trying to be better neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It used to be that outdoor dining, that sidewalk cafes could stay open until 1 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Then we modified it so that sidewalk cafes and roadway dining needed to close at midnight.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Today, we're shifting that to 11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In neighborhoods like mine, people live above restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: People live next door to restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it's important that we ensure that they're good neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: 11 o'clock is a very reasonable time to close, and I think we'll ensure that we can improve the quality of life in our communities.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're also going to insist that there's still meaningful accountability in the outdoor dining program.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If any restaurant...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: gets the same three violations in a two-year period, their license is revoked.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So when we have bad actors in our communities, we're going to hold them accountable.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We are also making sure that we continue to maintain the progress that we've made in keeping outdoor dining clean.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We all remember the era where there were rack complaints and garbage and storage.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's not going to happen again.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just this past year, with the new seasonal program, there were 11 complaints citywide to 311 about cleanliness of outdoor dining structures.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That number is so small, it's a rounding error.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You can't even see.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We have successfully improved cleanliness in our outdoor dining structures by ensuring all of the furniture is readily removable, that the floors have to be removed every single week, and area below it cleaned.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That all remains in place as we shift to a year-round program.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So we're not returning to the era of sheds.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We are maintaining the cleanliness that New Yorkers should and will continue to expect in our outdoor dining.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really want to thank Speaker Menon again for her leadership.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Her team, especially Jonathan, was incredibly helpful along the way.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We had a great support from the ledge staff, Rachel Cordero and Sarah Swain in particular.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Many advocates were real tremendous partners in this effort, especially Transportation Alternatives, Open Plans, the Hospitality Alliance, and others.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really am grateful to all of the small businesses across New York City that have advocated for these changes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But most of all, I just want to thank my chief of staff, Molly Haley, who is brilliant and is kind of the intellectual firepower that drives our office.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we're really lucky that she helped to drive this process forward.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you again and looking forward to it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Passing this bill today.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Menin introduces Intro 894A by Council Member Brewer, allowing sidewalk cafe operators to enclose year-round cafes annually from November 30 through March 31.
chapters.title: Menin introduces Brewer's sidewalk cafe enclosure bill

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's a great bill.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 894A, sponsored by Councilmember Gail Brewer, would allow sidewalk cafe operators to enclose their year-round sidewalk cafes annually from November 30th through March 31st.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I now want to invite Councilmember Brewer to talk about her bill.

chapters.summary: Brewer explains her bill makes it legal for sidewalk cafes to operate year-round with covers during cold months, helping restaurants maintain workforce and serve diners, and notes restaurants have a choice between seasonal and year-round options.
chapters.title: Brewer speaks on year-round sidewalk cafe enclosures

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You might have seen that at some situations, the outdoor cafe that's on the sidewalk, not the one that's the one in the roadway, has tables and chairs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But as soon as it gets cold, it goes in because there is no ability to stay out legally.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've seen some that are out there legally, but they're not.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're not.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're illegal.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so this bill would mandate that it is possible to be year-round.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And you could put, I would call it a cover, over the outdoor sidewalk cafe.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You sometimes go to a restaurant or a store and you'll see like a front door and it has cover.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It would be something similar to that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I have to say the reason we're doing it is similar to what Councilmember Ressler said, which is we want these restaurants to do well.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We want them to be able to maintain their workforce year-round so that they can, in fact, have good jobs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And we want to be sure that diners have the opportunity to be year-round.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Some of these restaurants obviously have both sidewalk and roadway, but most have...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: A sidewalk cafe.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's what we've known for years.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And the restaurant industry, hospitality lines in particular, is very happy about this bill because it makes it legal and makes it clear as to what you can or cannot do with your outdoor sidewalk cafe.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I'm very excited to have this.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think the fact that it

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: compliments what Councilmember Ressler, he forgot one point though.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The issue too is that people have a choice, remember that part?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You forgot that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They have a choice whether they want to have the roadway or not.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They can do seasonal, because some of the folks in my neighborhood, I called them at 11 o'clock at night.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What the hell are you doing?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're not making a choice?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And he said he is.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So thank you, Councilmember Ressler, for the choice.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is it seasonal or year-round?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Same with the Sidewalk Cafe.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You have a choice, but you can be legal, and you won't have to worry about tickets as long as you do the right thing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Brewer.

chapters.summary: Menin introduces Intro 917A by Council Member Sanchez requiring outdoor dining setups to be clear of trash and vermin, and Intro 918A by Council Member Thomas-Henry allowing quarterly installment payments for revocable consent fees.
chapters.title: Menin introduces Sanchez cleanliness bill and Thomas-Henry fee bill

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Also in this package is Introduction 917-A, sponsored by Councilmember Justin Sanchez, would require roadway and sidewalk cafe operators

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: to ensure that their outdoor setups are clear of trash, debris, graffiti, vermin, food scraps, and unsanitary conditions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I don't believe Councilmember Sanchez is here, but this is a great bill that really came out of a lot of the conversations that Councilmember Rester, Councilmember Brewer, many of us had with community groups that had raised concerns.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we really, I think, struck the balance.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: balance here between those quality of life concerns and supporting our small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then finally in the package, Introduction 918A, sponsored by Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry, would allow sidewalk and roadway cafe operators to pay their annual revocable consent fees in quarterly installments to reduce their upfront costs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I invite the Councilmember to talk about her bill.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry presents her first bill to pass, explaining how quarterly fee payments reduce upfront costs for restaurant owners and entrepreneurs, framing affordability as the cost to build a business and dream in NYC.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry speaks on quarterly fee installments for outdoor dining

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry, representing the 21st Council District in the World's Borough of Queens.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So imagine this for a moment.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The restaurant owner who takes a family recipe and turns it into a neighborhood favorite.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The immigrant entrepreneur who opens a storefront and in doing so creates a piece of home thousands of miles away from where they started.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The New Yorker who saves every dollar they can, takes a chance on themselves, signs a lease, turns on the lights, and says, I'm going to make this work.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That is the culture of small entrepreneurship in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And in diving into their dreams and sometimes fears, they bring their cultures, their perspectives, and their community with them.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Behind every one of those businesses is an entrepreneur with the grit, hustle, passion, and enough courage to not take no for an answer.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So when government has the opportunity to make that journey even easier, we should.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Today, I am incredibly proud that the council will vote on Intro 918, my first bill to pass in this body.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Intro 918 is simple.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Instead of requiring restaurants participating in our outdoor dining program to pay revocable consent fees to the city all at once, businesses will have the flexibility to make those payments quarterly.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The difference between an enormous bill and manageable payments throughout the year matters.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: During the pandemic, our entrepreneurs showed us what was possible.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They transformed sidewalks and streets into places of connection.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They kept people employed.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They fed our communities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They brought life back to neighborhoods during one of the darkest periods in our city's history.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We should not repay that ingenuity by putting unnecessary barriers in their way.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We should be asking ourselves every day, how do we make it easier for people in New York to stay here and succeed here?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Because affordability is not only about what it costs to live in New York, it is also about what it costs to build a life, build a business, and build a dream here.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Intro 918 is one step toward answering that question.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It says to our entrepreneurs, we see what it takes.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We value what you bring to our neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And what government is willing to meet you where you are.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And today I am proud that the council will take another step towards doing exactly that.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want to thank Speaker Menon for being an advocate for our small businesses and bringing this to a vote.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much, Council Member.

chapters.summary: Menin responds to a question about graffiti provisions, explaining the bills aim to help small businesses while addressing quality of life issues raised by community boards, striking a balance between support and accountability.
chapters.title: Q&A on graffiti concerns and quality of life balance in outdoor dining

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So that concludes our stated agenda.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We always want to be able to strike that balance.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But graffiti was one of the issues that came up time and time again in the community meetings that we had.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We heard from a lot of the community boards.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're not looking to penalize small business owners at all.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I think what you see from this package of bills, on the contrary, is we're really helping small business owners by fixing what was really a broken outdoor dining program and extending this to be year-round.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But we don't want to completely ignore quality of life issues that were brought to us.

chapters.summary: A reporter asks about the mayor's own reform proposals including shortening timelines and removing council veto power. Menin emphasizes the Council's focus on making it easier for small businesses to operate and working with the administration on shared goals.
chapters.title: Q&A on mayor's reform proposals and outdoor dining interaction

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Hi, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I have a question about, I'm sorry, Ethan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I'll let you go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Yeah, so the mayor has his own set of reforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: He said, you know, the code balance on the ballots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether you support those, some of those, take veto power away from the council, but the goal is to shorten the timeline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So, you know, I want to get your thoughts on that and how they interact with this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think what we're really focused on is trying to make it easier for small businesses to operate in New York.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I say this as someone who owned a restaurant, catering, and market in New York many, many years ago.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so it's not only this package of bills that's doing it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's also several weeks ago we passed Councilmember Susan Zhuang's bill to cut the red tape.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're really, really focused on that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will obviously be working closely with the administration on any ways that we can support our small businesses, making it easier for them to open, making it easier for them to operate, and making it easier for them to sustain and

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: not close, which is unfortunately what we've seen a lot in the last few years.

chapters.summary: Restler explains that at peak there were 8,000 roadway dining structures, now under 800, and expects significant new participation based on surveys showing cost was the top barrier. Menin adds concerns about DOT's slow permit approval process and the need for ongoing oversight.
chapters.title: Q&A on projected number of outdoor dining structures

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Is there a projection for how many more outdoor dining sheds, or not sheds, but structures there could be with this program in place now?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: At its peak, there were about 8,000 roadway dining structures in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Today, they're under 800.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We are confident, based on the surveys that we've seen of small businesses that have indicated that the number one reason they don't participate in the outdoor dining program is the cost

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: of constructing, deconstructing, and storing these outdoor dining sheds, that significant numbers of new businesses are going to participate in outdoor dining all across the city.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's, I think, premature to give a precise number on that, but we think this is going to have a significant effect on participation across the city.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It could very well be.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And, you know, I think to Kevin's earlier question, you know, it's also about improving the bureaucracy.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's been a really painful process for restaurants to interface with the Department of Transportation over the last few years, incredibly slow and challenging to get permits approved.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And, you know, while I support kind of creating uniformity between the sidewalk cafe and roadway dining application process, the COGE Commission also set really ambitious targets for streamlining the DOT approval process on the back end.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And the proof will be in the pudding whether they can actually deliver.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: whether they're going to invest in the additional staff, improve their management and their outcomes so that restaurants are able to participate more easily.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If DOT steps up and can deliver a more effective program, I think more restaurants will choose to participate as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And the only thing I want to just add on that is that, and that's really what oversight is for.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I used to chair the Consumer Protection Committee.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We had several oversight hearings when this program was rolled out.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In the first year of the program, I believe the statistic was only 10% of the small businesses had their full approval, not the conditional approval, but the full approval.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So to Councilmember Ressler's point, we're going to continue to monitor that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I frankly, from the outset, had concerns about giving an outdoor dining program to a transit agency, but that decision, that ship has sailed, and that decision was made several years ago.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: There's no more questions?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I can't hear.

chapters.summary: A reporter asks why the Council chose dispensers over raising fines like LA and Chicago did to $500. Menin explains that without enforcement staff, higher fines wouldn't deter behavior, and the holistic SCOOP Act approach targets the problem from multiple angles.
chapters.title: Q&A on dog waste fines vs. dispenser approach

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Hi, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you could talk about the decision to, specifically on the wastebasket bill, or the waste bag bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Can you talk about the decision to spend the money on that versus raising the fine?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I know Los Angeles and Chicago, they raised their dog fines to $500.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Was that a consideration at all?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The issue is no matter what the fine was, it was not deterring conduct because there's very little to no enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There is not enough enforcement staff to go out there and actually be able to enforce it and see it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And to Councilmember Brewer's point, it's very hard.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You have to actually catch someone in action, so to speak, and that can be really challenging to do.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we felt the best thing to do was this package of bills holistically, the Scoop Act, which is, you know, there's my bill, which, again, attaches the actual dog waste dispenser bags to over 1,200 litter baskets.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we're going to focus on areas that have the most dog waste complaints.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Then there are other components of the bill that focus on the package, that focus on public education.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So, again, we're trying to attack it from a multitude of different ways.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And the proof will be in the pudding.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're going to obviously monitor the complaints and see, are these bills working?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And if they're not lowering it, then we'll consider additional action.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But we want to do things that actually work.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And just raising the fine, there's not enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So that wouldn't, we don't believe.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Would have made a difference.

chapters.summary: Menin clarifies the bill covers 1,200 litter baskets, a compromise from the original version that would have covered every basket, and says this is a good start with focus on high-complaint areas.
chapters.title: Follow-up on waste bag dispenser scope: 1,200 baskets

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Well, again, this is going on 1,200 litter baskets.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's not on the original bill.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The original version had every single one.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We compromised there on 1,200, and we think that is a very good start.

chapters.summary: A reporter raises concerns about restaurants facing frequent inspections with rulers during construction. Menin says the bills don't address this but the Council is open to looking into it, and also notes concerns about health inspectors arriving during busy lunch service.
chapters.title: Q&A on outdoor dining inspection burdens and health inspector timing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Henry Ross, can we go back to the conversation about streamlining outdoor dining?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Does that also apply to when inspectors go out?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And let me explain what I mean.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I was just with a restaurant that went through the very cumbersome process of getting

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: roadway dining area and they say they see inspectors all the time literally coming out with rulers and stopping their work and getting into it does the bill streamline any of that sort of regulation because they say that's getting

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: really over the top for them

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yeah, the bills do not address that issue, but we're certainly happy to look at it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That was not something that came up, and we've had so many hearings, so many meetings.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That is not particularly a complaint that we heard, but we're certainly happy to look into it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And obviously anything that is becoming burdensome and cumbersome, we don't want to do.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We also, quite frankly, I think, need to look at the fact that inspectors are constantly coming from the health department during service.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So when you are having a busy lunch service, that is oftentimes when the health inspector will come, and that really puts an enormous burden on the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So for things, you know, whether they're measuring things, doing things, that's taking people away from their busiest time of service.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Any on-topic questions?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I think.

chapters.summary: Reporter Jesse asks what took so long to fix the outdoor dining program. Menin says she and others raised concerns from the start about giving the program to DOT and making it seasonal. Restler adds the Council is course-correcting quickly after seeing the program fail.
chapters.title: Q&A on timeline for outdoor dining legislative changes

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Hey, Jesse.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Hi, Jesse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jesse
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, I know this bill, or versions of the outdoor dining legislation have been introduced in the past.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jesse
utterances.text: And that previous or soon to be previous iteration of the program is pretty controversial and it seems like there's not a lot of fans in the council of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jesse
utterances.text: So I'm wondering what took so long for this change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jesse
utterances.text: Did the council just need fresh leadership?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, I'll start and then I'll turn it over to Councilmember Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, I, along with Councilmember Ressler and several others, when the council passed the original package, had raised a number of concerns.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I had raised the concern that I thought we should never be giving this program to DOT.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We should have given it to the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which has years of experience with sidewalk cafes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I also had raised the concern I thought it should be year-round because you're burdening these businesses, making them pay this enormous fee for six months, and then they have to store the tables and chairs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And most restaurants do not have the space or capacity to store this equipment.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we had raised those concerns.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The bill was passed, and then we saw what happened.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But let me turn it over to Councilmember Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just two points.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Firstly, and I think my colleagues here would agree, that reaching consensus on the temporary program

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: three years ago was one of the most challenging legislative, one of the most challenging bills that we navigated in the city council under Speaker Adams.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It was very contentious and there was a wide variety of concerns.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This process has been very different.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We've reached broad consensus that the program is not working and we need to fix it and that restoring year-round outdoor dining is necessary.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I would say that this is actually a really good example of government seeing something not working and fixing it and doing it pretty quickly.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The seasonal program was passed in late 2023.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It took 12 to 18 months for it to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And now, 12 plus months after that, we are...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Reforming it, and addressing what's not working.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That is what government should always be doing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We should be innovating, looking at trying to solve problems, and when things are not working, we fix it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We course correct.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I'm really proud that with Speaker Menon's leadership, we've been able to do that here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's clear that the seasonal program is not financially viable for restaurants across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's why 90% of them stop participating in it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're addressing that today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: off-topic questions.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'm sorry, related.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Oh, e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Okay, great.

chapters.summary: Menin explains e-bike registration is a state DMV issue, noting NYC DOT has said they lack authority and capacity. She mentions 17 e-bike related bills the Council is pursuing, including licensing third-party apps like DoorDash.
chapters.title: Off-topic Q&A on e-bike registration legislation

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, so a couple things.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I mean, first of all, the state of New Jersey just passed their e-bike legislation.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It was done on the state level, and it's done on the state level because of the state DMV.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: New York State, similarly, has their state DMV, which is really the agency that is appropriate to do any kind of registration.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And so certainly in conversations that have happened, even in the last council,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: around any kind of e-bike registration, it was made clear by the city Department of Transportation that they don't believe that they have the authority or the capacity to do the registration program.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And so I think there's pretty much uniform agreement around that, that it is a state issue.

chapters.summary: A reporter asks about speculation regarding independent expenditures from companies like DoorDash. Menin notes independent expenditures are by nature independent and declines to comment, highlighting the Council's work on licensing third-party delivery apps.
chapters.title: Off-topic Q&A on independent expenditures and DoorDash

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And then the second question, I don't know if you want to address speculation about independent expenditures, including policy proposals that you support specifically because of companies like DoorDash supporting your campaign.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Well, first of all, independent expenditures by their very nature are independent, something that any candidate, anyone running for office would have no comment on.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And I think what we're really doing with this e-bike legislation, we're doing 17 different bills that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We're also cracking down on enforcement, and we're also looking to license third-party apps like DoorDash.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So one of the bills, Councilmember Shulman's bill, will actually put the onus on DoorDash and other third-party apps and really crack down on some of their conduct.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Katie, you're up next.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

chapters.summary: Menin addresses concerns about BSA nominee John Manchin, noting some council members have raised concerns about his prior statements on community benefit agreements. She emphasizes the Council is pro-housing, having approved every ULURP and over 7,000 housing units, and looks forward to meeting Manchin.
chapters.title: Q&A on BSA nominee John Manchin and council housing concerns

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Happy to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And then I'm also going to ask our land use chair, Kevin Riley, and our majority whip and deputy speaker if they have anything to add on this.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So first of all, I've not met with John Manchin.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: He has not reached out yet for a meeting.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I look forward to meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: What we have heard from many council members are concerns about some of his prior statements.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We are a pro-housing council.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: This council has approved every single ULERP that has come before it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We have approved over 7,000 units of housing, over 3,000 of which are affordable.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So, again, any candidate to lead the BSA that will get our support must be adamantly pro-housing.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: What I think has happened in this situation, and this is why it's important to have advice and consent, is some members have raised some concerns about past writings of Mr.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Manchin that refer to community benefit agreements and other things that members have concerns about.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And so that will be the point of our hearing.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's the point of advice and consent, where there are questions, we raise them, we meet with the nominee, and we get our questions answered.

chapters.summary: Land Use Chair Kevin Riley defends the Council's housing record, citing Monitor Point as an example of finding consensus, and says concerns about Manchin's opposition to community benefit agreements are significant since CBAs help negotiate community needs during housing development.
chapters.title: Riley on council's pro-housing record and BSA nominee concerns

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And just want to share the same sentiment.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think as my role as land use chair, as chair of the zoning and franchise, I think my record speaks for itself, and I think the council's record speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We do our best with pushing housing projects through.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Even when it's turmoil within the community, we always try to find a yes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: An example of that is Monitor Point, which we worked with Councilmember Ressler to make sure that we got to the finish line.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think that's what the council has done.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So this perception that's online that this council is a NIMBY council, that's false.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: There's a lot of different concerns that members have with this nominee.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: When you talk about community benefits agreements, these are things that we negotiate with our communities when we are trying to build housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But we represent these communities.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We have to go back to these communities, and we realize what our communities need.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So these benefit agreements are supposed to benefit not only the community members that are there, but the new community members that are coming within our community.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And when you have such a high opposition to that, that's going to be a concern to a lot of members within the council.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So to answer your question, what is it going to take?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: It's going to take further conversations.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: It's going to take our hearing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We're going to see if John has the same ideologies that he did have when he made a lot of these statements.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But this council is a pro-housing council, and we want to make sure that we are addressing that concern as a council together.

chapters.summary: Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams details her concerns about Manchin's record conflicting with the Council's view of its powers, cites her Jamaica Neighborhood Plan with 12,000 units and 82 points of agreement, and emphasizes housing must come with infrastructure investment.
chapters.title: Williams on BSA nominee and community benefit agreements

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'll just say some of the concern that we have had as a council, you've already heard, is around his rhetoric, but also just his record.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I think a lot of the things he has been involved in, I personally see as in direct conflict with how the council sees its powers.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And we are a pro-housing council.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I often, as my homeowner colleagues, I'm often in the minority.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And do our homeowners need to be pushed to understand that there is a housing crisis and that we need to build more housing in every single district in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But that push needs to come with a give and take.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I was able to get 82 points of agreement from the administration through my neighborhood plan, which is essentially a community benefit agreement.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We are going to increase density, but through the increased density, we're going to also invest in infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We're going to invest in our parks.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We're going to invest in our arts and culture sector.

utterances.text: And those things make a community great.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We need to build housing, but we also need to think about other, I call them social and physical infrastructures that make a neighborhood what it is.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: My district has a sewer capacity issue.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so how can you build more units if you don't improve the sewer?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so those are the types of conversations that this council values.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And we're

utterances.text: We are not trying to negate housing, but we want to be at the table to have those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And some of the rhetoric and some of the things that have transpired in the past prevent us from being able to have those much-needed conversations.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So as Chair Riley said, I look forward to meeting John Manchin and having conversations with him.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I was told I didn't meet him, don't remember, but I look forward to meeting with him to learn more about how he sees the council's role.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Typically, council members do not play a role in what the BSA approves, and it'll be interesting to sort of understand how he sees his role as chair and whether or not he would be willing to listen to community and council member concerns as he would approve projects through the BSA.

summary: Finance Committee holds brief hearing to vote on a pre-considered transparency resolution (Res. 595) and a pre-considered intro (Intro 1002) establishing a temporary ECB judgment resolution program; both pass with Morano and Wong casting dissenting votes on respective items.

Speaker Julie Menin leads a pre-stated meeting press conference announcing the SCOOP Act dog waste package, outdoor dining reform bills, an Office of Insurance Affordability, an investigation into prediction market platforms targeting minors, and updates on immigrant protections including Rafael Rubio's asylum grant and Haitian TPS termination.

Council members present legislation on Staten Island flag codification, firearm discharge reporting, certification of no harassment, dog waste education and composting, year-round outdoor dining, and quarterly fee installments, followed by Q&A on outdoor dining projections, enforcement, BSA nominee concerns, and consumer protection.
title: Committee on Finance
topic: Establish a temporary program to resolve outstanding judgments imposed by the environmental control board
